\chapter{Ten Words, Ninety-Nine Numbers}
\label{ch:zh-decimal}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build any number from eleven to ninety-nine out of the ten words I already have, say a hundred, and read a price written in Arabic numerals.}

One rule of order turns ten words into ninety-nine numbers, \zh{一百} is where \zh{一}'s tone finally moves, and the digits chapter says which of 5 and \zh{五} a price tag actually prints.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[shíyī]{\zh{十一} — eleven, and the teens in one line}

\label{lesson:ZH-C21-shiyi}



\begin{quote}
Count one to ten, then say ten on its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — ten, then one}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{十一}} — \emph{shíyī} — \textbf{eleven}
\end{quote}

Ten, then one. That is all of it.

And it does not stop at eleven. \textbf{\zh{十五}} is \emph{shíwǔ}, ten-five, fifteen. \textbf{\zh{十九}} is \emph{shíjiǔ}, ten-nine, nineteen. English has \emph{eleven}, \emph{twelve}, \emph{thirteen} — three separate shapes before the pattern starts — and German, Russian and Urdu each have their own nine irregular words to memorise here.

\textbf{Mandarin has none. The teens are the numbers you already have, in the order you already say them.} Nine numbers, no new vocabulary, no new characters, and nothing to learn but the order.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{shíyī} — eleven
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{shí} + \textbf{sān} $\to$ \textbf{shísān}, thirteen
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{shí} + \textbf{bā} $\to$ \textbf{shíbā}, eighteen
  \item \emph{Run through:} eleven to nineteen, straight through
\end{itemize}

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}

\section[èrshí]{\zh{二十} — twenty, and ninety-nine numbers from ten words}

\label{lesson:ZH-C21-ershi}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{shíyī}, and build seventeen.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — turn the pair round}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{二十}} — \emph{èrshí} — \textbf{twenty}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\zh{十一}} is ten-one, eleven. \textbf{\zh{二十}} is two-ten, twenty. The same two words in the other order, and the order is the entire difference.

That gives every ten: \textbf{\zh{三十}} thirty, \textbf{\zh{四十}} forty, \textbf{\zh{九十}} ninety. Put a unit on the end of one and you have everything between: \textbf{\zh{二十一}}, \emph{èrshíyī}, twenty-one; \textbf{\zh{九十九}}, ninety-nine.

\textbf{Ten words reach ninety-nine.} English needs \emph{eleven}, \emph{twelve} and \emph{thirteen} before its own pattern begins, and \emph{twenty}, \emph{thirty} and \emph{fifty} are three more shapes again. Mandarin needs none of them.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{九十九}}, ninety-nine, is the drill this book has been waiting for. \emph{jiǔ} is third tone and so is the \emph{jiǔ} at the end, and the rule you met in chapter 1 applies: a third tone before another third tone lifts and becomes a rise.

Say it: \textbf{jiú-shí-jiǔ}. The first nine rises, the last one dips.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{èrshí} — twenty
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{sān} + \textbf{shí} $\to$ \textbf{sānshí}, thirty
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{wǔ} + \textbf{shí} + \textbf{liù} $\to$ \textbf{wǔshíliù}, fifty-six
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jiúshíjiǔ} — ninety-nine, with the first dip lifted
\end{itemize}

\section[bǎi]{\zh{百} — a hundred, on a box you have built before}

\label{lesson:ZH-W21-bai}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{四} and \zh{一}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — six strokes, five of them familiar}
\begin{quote}
\zh{百}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Six strokes. For a hundred.}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the top \textbf{héng} horizontal, left to right
  \item lift, then the short \textbf{piě} below it, falling to the left
  \item lift, then the \textbf{shù} vertical down the left side of the box
  \item lift, then the \textbf{héngzhé}: across the top of the box and down its right side
  \item lift, then the inner \textbf{héng} horizontal
  \item lift, then the bottom \textbf{héng}, closing the box
\end{enumerate}

Strokes 3 to 6 are the box of \textbf{\zh{四}}, built in the same order: the left side, then the top-and-right turn, then the inside, then the floor. \textbf{Outside before inside, and the box closes last} — the rule you used for \zh{四} and \zh{口}.

Only strokes 1 and 2 are new, and stroke 1 is \zh{一}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{百} — bar, short fall, then the box in \zh{四}'s order
  \item \zh{四} beside it and mark the four strokes they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[yìbǎi]{\zh{一百} — a hundred, and \zh{一} moves}

\label{lesson:ZH-C21-bai}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{百}, then say twenty.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{百}} \emph{bǎi} means \textbf{a hundred}, and it is almost always said with \zh{一} in front of it: \textbf{\zh{一百}}, one hundred.

\textbf{bǎi} is \textbf{third tone}, the low dip, like \emph{jiǔ} and \emph{wǔ}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
Counting on its own, \zh{一} is \textbf{yī}, high and level. In \textbf{\zh{一百}} it is not: you say \textbf{yìbǎi}, with a fall.

\zh{一} shifts its tone depending on what follows, exactly as \textbf{\zh{不}} does — the behaviour this book named in its first chapter for a different word. Before a first, second or third tone, \zh{一} falls: \textbf{yìbǎi}. Before a fourth tone it rises instead.

So the number that sounds simplest in the run is the one that changes most, and a hundred is where a learner meets it first.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yī} alone — level
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yìbǎi} — falling, then dipping
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{shí, èrshí, yìbǎi} — ten, twenty, a hundred
\end{itemize}

\section[wǔ]{5 and \zh{五} — the same number, two registers}

\label{lesson:ZH-C21-digits}



\begin{quote}
Say five, then say a hundred.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — where each one is written}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{5} and \textbf{\zh{五}} are both \emph{wǔ}.
\end{quote}

A reader who has spent this chapter learning \zh{六} \zh{七} \zh{八} \zh{九} \zh{十} could still walk past a Chinese shop and read nothing on the price tag, because \textbf{a price is written in Arabic numerals}. So are dates, telephone numbers, bus numbers, floor numbers, addresses and the year.

The characters are not archaic. They are a different register, and both are current:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written with} & \textbf{where you meet it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{5}, \textbf{20}, \textbf{100} & prices, dates, phone numbers, addresses, anything counted \\
\textbf{\zh{五}}, \textbf{\zh{二十}}, \textbf{\zh{一百}} & formal and legal text, cheque amounts, shop signs, set phrases, running prose \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both are read aloud \textbf{the same way} — you see \textbf{5} and you say \emph{wǔ}. That is the useful part: the digits cost you nothing to learn and everything to ignore.

One convention worth carrying: on a bill or a cheque an amount is often written twice, once in digits and once in characters, because the characters are much harder to alter.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{5}, \textbf{10}, \textbf{20}, \textbf{99} aloud as \emph{wǔ}, \emph{shí}, \emph{èrshí}, \emph{jiúshíjiǔ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} each of those four in characters as well
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of the two a price tag uses, and which a cheque uses
\end{itemize}

\section[Practice]{Payoff — ninety-nine numbers, and the price tag}

\label{lesson:ZH-C21-practice}



\begin{quote}
Count one to ten, then say which of \textbf{5} and \textbf{\zh{五}} a price tag uses.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Build, do not recall.} Say twelve, seventeen, thirty, forty-five, sixty-eight and eighty-one, from the ten words alone.
  \item Say \textbf{jiúshíjiǔ}, ninety-nine, with the first dip lifted.
  \item Say \textbf{yìbǎi}, and say what happens to \zh{一} in front of it.
  \item Read \textbf{8}, \textbf{15}, \textbf{30}, \textbf{99} and \textbf{100} off a page and say each aloud.
  \item Write \textbf{\zh{十一}}, \textbf{\zh{二十}} and \textbf{\zh{一百}} in characters.
  \item Give a floor number, an age and a price, each as a bare number.
\end{enumerate}

Count what this cost: \textbf{five characters and one rule of order} — ten before a unit multiplies nothing, ten after a unit multiplies it. That order is worth more than every word in this chapter put together.

What is still out of reach: \emph{yìqiān}, a thousand, and everything above it — and the measure word a Chinese number needs before an actual noun, which is a chapter of its own.

\section[Practice]{Close the numeral slice}

\label{lesson:ZH-R21-close}



\begin{quote}
Count one to ten, then say why eight costs more.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
The six new characters, alone, from spoken cues and with no number around them: \textbf{\zh{六} \zh{七} \zh{八} \zh{九} \zh{十} \zh{百}}.

Then put each back to work once.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Write the five single digits and say the stroke count of each. Four, two, two, two, two — twelve strokes for five numbers.
  \item Write \textbf{\zh{百}} and mark the four strokes it shares with \textbf{\zh{四}}.
  \item Write \textbf{\zh{早}} and mark the \textbf{\zh{十}} inside it.
  \item Write \textbf{\zh{人}} and \textbf{\zh{八}} side by side and say what separates them.
  \item Build six numbers between eleven and ninety-nine from the ten words.
  \item Read a price in digits and say it aloud in words.
\end{enumerate}

Say what the whole slice cost the hand: \textbf{six characters, fourteen strokes}, and one rule about the order of two of them.
